[Clinical segment 1] A 65-year-old man with a history of hepatitis B, hepatitis C, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity presented with several months of facial swelling, dysphagia, and dysarthria. Shortly thereafter, he developed a pruritic rash on his trunk and upper extremities. He did not report a personal or family history of angioedema. His medications included lisinopril, atorvastatin, albuterol, and ibuprofen for rheumatoid arthritis. The patient had discontinued etanercept six months before presentation. He presented to the emergency department two weeks after seeing his primary care provider for a persistent periorbital, chest, and upper extremity rash. His rash worsened, and he noted new throat swelling and weakness.

[Clinical segment 2] - Laboratory Tests: - Basic metabolic panel and complete blood count were unremarkable - Elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate - Negative viral respiratory panel - C4, C1q, and C1 esterase inhibitor were unremarkable - Normal serum and urine protein electrophoresis - Elevated transaminases - Elevated anti-Sjögren syndrome–related antigen A autoantibodies - High antinuclear antibody titers - Negative anti-Jo antibody - Elevated creatine kinase - Positive myositis panel for anti-SAE antibodies - Imaging Studies: - CT neck: Mild submental inflammatory stranding with no discrete fluid collection or abscess - Liver ultrasound: Hepatic steatosis - CT chest: Multiple nodular and airspace opacities, including right lower lobe nodule - Pathology: - Skin biopsy results were consistent with Wong-type presentation

[Clinical segment 3] Vital signs were stable on arrival. Physical examination was notable for anasarca and a diffuse coalescent erythematous rash over the extremities, chest, and abdomen, with scaling and crusting of the back. There was a heliotrope rash and erythematous lip swelling. He had weakness to resistance in all extremities and a muffled voice without tongue swelling. Over several days, the patient's shoulder and hip weakness progressed, and he could not lift his arms above his head or stand without assistance.

[Clinical segment 1] On examination, blood pressure was 113/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Abdominal, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 13 mm gestational sac with irregular margins and a yolk sac in the anterior isthmic portion of the uterus, raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy. Doppler was declined. Serial β-hCG measurements rose by 33% over 48 hours (21,521 mIU/mL). The patient missed follow-up and returned 1 week later with 5 days of worsening pelvic pain.

[Clinical segment 2] Repeat transvaginal scan revealed a fetal pole with cardiac activity (crown–rump length 0.9 cm) in a sac traversing the full width of the anterior myometrium, extending exophytically toward the serosa, with trophoblastic flow on Doppler; there was no endometrial fluid or free pelvic fluid. She was taken to laparoscopy and hysteroscopy: the bladder was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, the ectopic was not visualized, and extensive intrauterine adhesions obscured the view; there was no intracavitary bleeding. Postoperatively, she became hypotensive (systolic 82–95 mmHg) without vaginal bleeding. This prompted an urgent MRI to map the location of the pregnancy.

[Clinical segment 3] A 36-year-old G5P2+2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries and two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 6 weeks of amenorrhea for evaluation of a pregnancy of unknown location. Her serum quantitative β-hCG was 16,124 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound at presentation did not locate an intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy. A copper intrauterine device had been removed 2 months before her last menstrual period. She had used one cycle of clomiphene. She had no chronic illnesses, did not smoke or drink, and was not on medications.

[Clinical segment 1] An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative.

[Clinical segment 2] Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal.

[Clinical segment 3] Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory.

[Clinical segment 4] Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

input_text: [Clinical segment 1] An 87-year-old Cantonese-speaking man with Alzheimer’s dementia, hypertension, stroke, hyperlipidaemia, gout, peptic ulcer, and chronic kidney disease presented with one week of increasing left leg pain and weakness, impaired mobility, and a single episode of urinary incontinence. He also reported anorexia and a 12% body-weight loss over six months. On examination, his blood pressure was 88/45 mmHg (responsive to IV fluids), heart rate 96/min, temperature 36.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He weighed 51 kg (BMI 19 kg/m2). Cardiac and chest examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination was normal. Neurologic examination showed 4/5 strength in left hip and knee flexors and extensors; the rest of the exam was normal. Initial laboratory results demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 76 mg/L, WCC 11.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.5 × 10^9/L) and pre-renal acute-on-chronic kidney injury. An initial differential of cauda equina syndrome or epidural abscess prompted an urgent MRI of the lumbar spine, which showed mild foraminal narrowing at L5–S1 but no central canal stenosis or abscess. He was admitted for possible sepsis; chest X-ray, atypical pneumonia serology, and urine microscopy and culture were all unremarkable. A plain X-ray of the left hip showed no fracture. Despite analgesia, his left hip pain worsened, strength declined to 2/5 at the hip and 3/5 at the knee, and CRP and ESR continued to rise. A left hip ultrasound revealed a small anterior joint effusion. Normal tumour markers, MRI of the hip, and an isotope bone scan argued against malignancy. Attempts at hip aspiration were unsuccessful. Colchicine was started for presumed crystal arthropathy and atorvastatin was discontinued for possible myopathy, but creatine kinase was normal, and symptoms persisted. An MRI of the hips and pelvis then demonstrated bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas muscle oedema with enhancement and a left-sided insertional tendinopathy, with no evidence of trochanteric bursitis.

input_text: [Clinical segment 1] A 65-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presented for urologic evaluation. His prostate-specific antigen level was 0.796 ng/mL. Uroflowmetry revealed reduced urine flow, prolonged micturition time, and obstructive findings. He was started on oral Alfuzosin 10 mg once daily. On day 9 of therapy, he reported loss of appetite and malaise, followed by generalized pruritus, dark urine, and jaundice. He denied use of aspirin, acetaminophen, or herbal medicines and had no history of liver disease. On examination, he was jaundiced but had no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory studies showed leukocyte count 5.8 K/μL, AST 175 U/L (0–40), ALT 402 U/L (0–55), alkaline phosphatase 235 U/L (15–250), γ-glutamyl transferase 327 U/L (8–61), total bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL (0.2–1.2), and direct bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL (0–0.25). Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal liver, gallbladder, common bile duct, and intrahepatic bile ducts. Serologic tests for HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV, anti-HAV IgM, anti-HEV, HEV RNA, and HCV RNA were negative. Autoimmune markers (ANA, AMA, ASMA, LKM-1) were negative. Metabolic evaluations—including transferrin saturation, ferritin, alpha-1 antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, and ophthalmologic exam for Kayser–Fleischer rings—were normal. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a normal biliary anatomy.

input_text: [Clinical segment 1] A 65-year-old woman presented with right dorsal pain. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 452 IU/L, and γ-glutamyl transferase 167 IU/L. The indocyanine green plasma disappearance rate was 0.103, and the 15-minute retention rate was 23.9%, indicating depressed liver function. Tests for hepatitis B and C viral markers were negative. Serum levels of α-fetoprotein, PIVKA-II, CEA, and CA19-9 were within normal limits; DUPAN-2 was 200 U/mL, CA125 was 321.8 U/mL, and neuron-specific enolase was 29.2 ng/mL. Abdominal CT revealed a well-defined, low-density, heterogeneous, multilocular cystic tumor with septa replacing the right hepatic lobe and medial segment of the left lobe, measuring 16 cm in diameter, with an enhancing solid compartment and a nonenhancing cystic compartment, compressing the umbilical portion of the portal vein, the right portal vein, and the left hepatic vein. MRI showed mixed high and low signal intensity: cysts were low on T1-weighted images and high on T2-weighted images, and areas of high T1 and low T2 signal suggested intratumoral hemorrhage. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a honeycomb-like tumor with solid components. PET–CT showed FDG uptake in the solid components of the cyst. From these imaging findings, the preoperative diagnosis of mucinous cystadenocarcinoma or sarcoma of the liver was made.

input_text: [Clinical segment 1] A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with bilateral breast lumps of one-week duration. Cytologic diagnosis was duct cell carcinoma of both breasts with left axillary lymph node metastasis. A core-needle biopsy of the left breast confirmed infiltrative duct cell carcinoma that was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive. On the basis of the physical examination results, the right breast lump was suspected to be a fibroadenoma. Hence, lumpectomy was performed.

[Clinical segment 2] A 27-year-old woman who works as an agricultural laborer was referred with fatigue, malaise, anorexia, and epistaxis. On examination, she was pale, with eczematous plaques on her chest and proximal right arm, and had splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, white-cell count 4.0×10^9/L, and platelets 23×10^9/L. A peripheral-blood smear revealed lymphoblasts. Flow cytometry was positive for TdT, CD34, CD19, CD10, CD22, and HLA-DR, and bone marrow evaluation confirmed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The eczematous plaques were treated as contact dermatitis with topical methylprednisolone, resolving rapidly, and induction chemotherapy with hyper-CVAD was initiated.

input_text: [Clinical segment 1] A 28-year-old Hispanic man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis presented with a 10-day history of a pruritic eruption that began on the trunk and gradually spread to all extremities. He denied contact allergens, fever, or hyperhidrosis and had no prior history of atopic dermatitis, dermatophytosis, or hand eczema. On examination, he had scleral icterus and multiple dusky, thin plaques with a central collarette of scale on the face, neck, axillae, trunk, and extremities. On both hands and feet, there were hyperkeratotic plaques and deeply seated vesicles with a greenish-black hue, especially accentuated along the dermatoglyphic ridges. Laboratory testing showed total bilirubin 28.9 mg/dL (reference <1.2), direct bilirubin 17.7 mg/dL (<0.3), AST 78 IU/L, ALT 42 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 231 IU/L. A punch biopsy of the right palm revealed psoriasiform epidermal acanthosis, intraepidermal spongiosis, hyperkeratosis with sparse perivascular lymphocytic inflammation, and a dilated eccrine duct containing amorphous pink material. Gram, periodic acid–Schiff, and iron stains were negative. Punch biopsies of the chest and thigh were consistent with pityriasis rosea.

input_text: [Clinical segment 1] A 48-year-old woman with no breast symptoms underwent routine screening mammography, which demonstrated a new 1.4-cm developing asymmetry in the inner quadrant of the right breast on craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique views. Targeted breast ultrasonography at the 4:00 position, 4 cm from the nipple, showed no discrete abnormality corresponding to the mammographic finding. Because the asymmetry persisted, a tomosynthesis-guided vacuum-assisted biopsy of the right inner breast was performed, yielding 12 core specimens. Histologic examination revealed marked perilobular and periductal mixed chronic inflammatory infiltrate enriched in eosinophils, with lymphocytes and plasma cells and no granulomata. The Allergy and Immunology service noted that the patient was asymptomatic, with no history of urticaria, asthma, angioedema, or pruritus except for seasonal allergic rhinitis. Peripheral blood eosinophil levels were within the normal range. Hypereosinophilic syndrome was excluded from consideration.

input_text: [Clinical segment 1] A 52-year-old South Asian man presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging swelling of the left cheek. On examination, there was a diffuse, firm, non-tender mass measuring about 4 × 5 cm that extended from the infraorbital region superiorly to the lip commissure inferiorly, medially obliterating the nasal ala, and laterally approaching the preauricular area. Intraoral examination revealed a well-defined vestibular swelling measuring 4 × 3 cm, extending from the distal aspect of the left canine to the second molar. Routine hematologic parameters were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a mildly homogeneously enhancing soft-tissue density lesion in the left premaxillary region with adjacent bony destruction of the maxillary alveolus. Based on the clinical findings, a provisional diagnosis of malignancy of the left maxilla was made, and the differential diagnosis included benign tumor, sarcoma, lymphoma, and melanoma. An incisional biopsy suggested myositis with lymphoid hyperplasia.

Sarcoma was considered due to the bony destruction seen on CT

response.rationale: Biopsy suggests myositis with lymphoid hyperplasia, favoring an inflammatory pseudotumor over malignant neoplasm; the homogeneous enhancement and bony destruction are consistent with an inflammatory mass.

[Clinical segment 1] At 1 week of age, examination of the eyes showed very weak light reflexes bilaterally. The anterior chambers were slightly shallow, but there were no pupillary abnormalities, cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus, or ptosis. Funduscopic examination revealed mild optic nerve pallor with suspected peripapillary double-ring sign. The fundus had a faint reddish tone; retinal vessels appeared normal in caliber and reached the periphery. No chorioretinal dysplasia was noted.

[Clinical segment 2] A female infant was born at 35 weeks 4 days’ gestation, weighing 2152 g. She was one of monochorionic diamniotic twins; her identical twin died in utero at 24 weeks. Fetal ultrasound had shown microcephaly and ventricular enlargement. Postnatal MRI of the head revealed microcephaly, marked enlargement of both lateral ventricles without signs of elevated intracranial pressure, and severe thinning of the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes; the temporal lobes, basal ganglia, thalamus, brain stem, and cerebellum were preserved. No intracranial hematoma or neoplastic lesions were seen. Family history was noncontributory.
